Items.Authors: Laura Manuela Castañeda Medina, Yann Gutierrez, Baptiste Abeloos, Olivier Herscovici-Schiller, Johan Mazoyer, Laurent M. Mugnier
Items.Title: Reinforcement learning for post-coronagraphic wavefront control
Items.Abstract: Direct imaging of exoplanets is limited by the extreme contrast between the star and the planets, which is mitigated using a coronagraph.   However, optical aberrations cause starlight leakage through the coronagraph, producing speckles that obscure the planetary signal. Achieving the required contrast levels demands wavefront control with subnanometric precision.   Deep reinforcement learning, offers a promising alternative to traditional wavefront control approaches. In this work, we present a fully data-driven method for post-coronagraphic aberration correction from focal plane images using reinforcement learning. The agent directly controls a deformable mirror in the pupil plane using phase diversity images generated via single actuator probes. The method is validated on simplified simulations of a high-contrast imaging testbed, where it successfully created the first Dark Holes using reinforcement learning.

Items.Authors: Simon Carrier, Jean-Pierre Véran, Maaike van Kooten, Kate Jackson, Jean-François Pratte, Serge Charlebois
Items.Title: Time-resolved pyramid wavefront sensor experimental results on REVOLT AO bench
Items.Abstract: Pyramid wavefront sensors (PWFS) offer excellent sensitivity, but suffer from non-linear behavior. This is typically mitigated by modulating the guide star image around the pyramid’s apex, which improves linearity but reduces sensitivity.    We are developing a Time-Resolved Pyramid Wavefront Sensor (TR-PWFS) that leverages the high temporal resolution of our SPAD-based detectors to break the modulation cycle into discrete time frames. By processing these frames individually, we improve robustness to detector noise and get higher AO performance.    In this paper, we will present on-sky results of the TR-PWFS on the PWFS arm of the REVOLT AO bench using a commercial SPAD-based camera with the aim of running 500Hz. In addition, we will report simulation results showing how the TR-PWFS offers advantages compared to the typical modulated and unmodulated PWFS for NPCAs and petaling errors in segmented-pupil systems.

Items.Authors: Maclean Rouble, Michel Adamic, Matt Dobbs, Joshua Montgomery, Ketan Sand, Sofiia Savchyn, Graeme Smecher
Items.Title: A kilo-pixel array of microwave kinetic inductance detectors operated with electro-quasiparticle feedback
Items.Abstract: As the technological readiness of microwave kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) advances, a major opportunity for progress towards achieving instrument-level background-limited performance lies in the manner in which arrays of these detectors are operated. We have previously demonstrated an in-situ technique to address limitations encountered when operating highly multiplexed arrays by altering and maintaining the resonant frequency of individual KIDs under changing loads using fast, active, electro-quasiparticle feedback. This is implemented as a control loop which digitally modulates the readout current to feed back directly on the quasiparticle and supercurrent systems of the KID to guarantee optimal biasing, maintain spectral purity, and eliminate operational inter-resonator collisions.  We present results from the first use of this technique at deployment scale using a kilo-pixel KID array, and discuss its implications for effective array yield, responsivity, linearity, and noise.

Items.Authors: Philipp A. Huber, Kimi Spirig, Felix A. Dannert, Adrian M. Glauser, Sascha P. Quanz
Items.Title: Constraining planetary orbital parameters with the Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE)
Items.Abstract: The Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE) is a planned space-based nulling interferometer designed to directly detect and characterize temperate, terrestrial exoplanets in the Solar neighborhood. Unlike classical imaging instruments, LIFE does not record spatially resolved images but instead its observable is a time-domain signal. Data reduction therefore relies on matching the data with pre-calculated templates that depend on the planetary position. Previous studies have assumed planets to remain static with respect to their host stars during an observation, an approximation that breaks down in certain scenarios like the observation of habitable-zone planets around M-dwarfs.  We present first work on the impact of planetary orbital motion on data reduction and means to address it. We further investigate LIFE's ability to constrain the orbital parameters from single observations as a function of integration time, a factor relevant for mission scheduling and instrument definition.

Items.Authors: Clark E. Baker, John S. Young, Martin Fisher, Samantha J. Thompson, Eugene Seneta, Alireza Esmaeilzadeh, Didier Queloz, Peter Pedersen, Tim Naylor, Ian Wellaway, Jay Fitzpatrick, Tomáš Turek, Martin Šulc, Petr Kačer, Alberto Madrigal Aguado, Andrew W. Ridings, Carlos Martín Perez, Cecilia Fariña, Chris Benn, Don Abrams, Eduardo Mantero, Frank Gribbin, Joel Concepción, Judith Santos-Torres, Jure Skvarc, Kevin Dee, Lara Monteagudo, Lucía Suárez-Andrés, Luis Hernández, Marc Balcells, Nada Ihanec, Neil O'Mahony, Roberto Martínez, Rubén Sánchez Janssen
Items.Title: The roboticisation of the Isaac Newton Telescope: the largest robotic telescope in the world
Items.Abstract: In this publication, we are happy to announce the successful roboticization of the 2.54m Isaac Newton Telescope (INT). The INT has been thoroughly refurbished and serviced; this includes: new motors and encoders for the telescope, dome and shutters, a meteorological weather station with an extensive suite of sensors, a complete telescope control system which interacts with instrumentation control software, and a series of safety systems for both equipment and personnel. The robust, reliable and accurate core mechanical ‘bones’ and optics of the INT remain. This comprehensive overhaul brings the INT to modern standards and enables it to operate completely autonomously. Great effort has been made to maximise the reliability of the system, with long mean time to failure and low mean time to repair. It is foreseen that this upgrade will enable the INT to operate efficiently and effectively for many decades to come.

Items.Authors: Christopher Layden, John Piotrowski, Kevin B. Burdge, Jack T. Dinsmore, Gábor Furész, Juliana Garcia-Mejia, David Osip, Roger Romani
Items.Title: Lightspeed: ultra-fast multicolor imaging and polarimetry on the Magellan Clay Telescope
Items.Abstract: Lightspeed will be a wide field (7'x4'), high-speed (>100Hz full frame, >10kHz windowed), multicolor (ugriz + future IR) imager and polarimeter. Employing Hamamatsu ORCA-Quest 2 cameras, Lightspeed will achieve deep sub-electron read noise (0.28 e-), making it incredibly powerful for high speed or ultra-faint observations. Lightspeed's VIS-POL channel will use a wedged double Wollaston prism, allowing linear polarization measurement in every frame. Lightspeed is currently under development and is planned to be a facility instrument on the Magellan Clay telescope. We recently commissioned proto-Lightspeed, a single channel prototype using off-the-shelf optical components which is now a PI instrument on Clay. I will discuss the design of Lightspeed and the performance of proto-Lightspeed, including characterization of the CMOS image sensors employed for both instruments.

Items.Authors: Johan Mazoyer, María Jesús Mellado Tenorio, Axel Potier, Christian Wilkinson, Pierre Baudoz, Raphaël Galicher, Iva Laginja, Lukas Delaye
Items.Title: Coherence differential imaging using random forest regression for the direct detection of exoplanets
Items.Abstract: Coronagraphic imaging of exoplanets is limited by residual speckles that mimic planets. Advanced post-processing is essential for current and future instruments on the ground or in space.  Current techniques are time-intensive and limited. ADI requires long sequences and is limited at small separation. RDI is also time-consuming and sensitive to speckle evolution, leading to imperfect subtraction. Coherence Differential Imaging (CDI) offers a faster alternative by using the light incoherence between speckles and planets, but its reliance on accurate instrumental models limits performance.  After demonstration on SPHERE, we enhanced CDI with a Random Forest algorithm. This method models the differential signal as a high-dimensional regression problem, optimizing the discrimination between coherent speckle noise and the incoherent planet signal. We validate this enhanced CDI using testbed data reproducing Roman CGI conditions.

Items.Authors: Matthijs Mars, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Jared R. Males, Joseph D. Long, Laird M. Close, Kyle Van Gorkom, Olivier Guyon, Alexander Hedglen, Parker T. Johnson, Maggie Y. Kautz, Jay K. Kueny, Rico Landman, Joshua Liberman, Miles Lucas, Jennifer Lumbres, Eden A. McEwen, Avalon McLeod, Tiffany Nguyen, Logan A. Pearce, Lauren Schatz, Elena Tonucci, Katie Twitchell, Alycia J. Weinberger
Items.Title: Non-linear low-order wavefront control with a physics-based digital twin: on-sky results from MagAO-X
Items.Abstract: We present a fully physics-based, differentiable digital twin of the focal-plane low-order wavefront sensor (FLOWFS) system on MagAO-X. This optical model enables both non-linear reconstruction of low-order aberrations and the derivation of a linear interaction matrix for high-speed (8 kHz) low-order control on-sky. By maintaining a stable wavefront at the coronagraph, we reduce stellar leakage and improve coronagraphic performance. Because the model is fully physics-based, it remains robust across changing observing conditions and transitions cleanly from laboratory to on-sky operation. It can also be rapidly adapted to different filters or coronagraph masks with minimal recalibration.

Items.Authors: Olivier Perdereau, Daniel Charlet, Cedric Esnault, Monique Taurigna, Reza Ansari, Cédric Dumez-Viou, Paul-Eric Pottie, Hadrien Grasland
Items.Title: On-sky performances measurements of the IDROGEN boards with the PAON4 radio interferometer
Items.Abstract: PAON4 is a 4 dishes radio interferometer installed at the Nancay Radio Observatory. This small array is devoted at demonstrating the effectiveness of data-taking, observing strategy and data analysis techniques for low-z (Z<.6) cosmology with the 21cm intensity mapping, using a large, compact array observing in transit mode. After a first phase ended in 2019, its acquisition system is now being upgraded with Idrogen boards. These generic digital electronics boards built around an Altera FPGA implement the white Rabbit timing system. They are complemented in our application by FMC mezzanine boards with 2 channel 1Gsamples/s ADCs. I'll review the in-lab tests we made to check the performances of the system, in particular the timing accuracy and stability, in which we observed am excellent stability and accuracy (within ~+/- 5ps peak to peak, over more than 50h). I'll show some technical details of their installation in the PAON4 system, and results from the first on sky observations.

Items.Authors: Giovanni Isopi, Alessandro Attoli, Eleonora Barbavara, Elia S. Battistelli, Paolo de Bernardis, Federico Cacciotti, Giuseppe Carboni, Ettore Carretti, Daniele Ciccalotti, Fabio Columbro, Alessandro Coppolecchia, Angelo Cruciani, Giuseppe D'Alessandro, Marco De Petris, Sofia Ferazzoli, Federica Govoni, Adelaide Ladu, Luca Lamagna, Pasqualino Marongiu, Silvia Masi, Matteo Murgia, Alessandro Navarrini, Alessandro Novelli, Andrea Occhiuzzi, Andrea Orlati, Alessandro Paiella, Giorgio Pettinari, Francesco Piacentini, Mauro Pili, Tonino Pisanu, Sergio Poppi, Luca Schirru, Gian Paolo Vargiu
Items.Title: MISTRAL: first light from the Sardinia Radio Telescope and status of the technical commissioning
Items.Abstract: MISTRAL is a novel multi-beam cryogenic camera observing from the Sardinia Radio Telescope (SRT) in the W-band. It features a wide 4 arcminute field of view sampled by 415 KIDs, sensitive to continuum radiation in the 77-103 GHz band. Coupled to the 64m dish of SRT with a custom cold (4K) re-imaging system, it produces a beamwidth of 12 arcseconds. The high sensitivity and wide field of view makes MISTRAL suitable for wide area continuum surveys in the W band, capabilities shared by few instruments in the world installed on large radio telescopes. In this contribution, we report the status of the commissioning of MISTRAL after the first year of observations from the SRT, in preparation to the opening to proposals from the scientific community. We will report the on-sky performance of the instrument with the initial high-frequency configuration of the SRT, its resolution and wide area scanning capabilities, showing the first light maps from the commissioning runs.

Items.Authors: Sagi Ben-Ami, Eran O. Ofek, Ofer Yaron, Oren Ironi, Yahel Sofer-Rimalt, Arie Blumenzweig, Daniel Golod, David Polishook, Andy Galasso
Items.Title: The Multi-Aperture Spectroscopic Telescope: a novel telescope array at the Weizmann Astrophysical Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Multi-Aperture Spectroscopic Telescope (MAST) is a new, fiber-fed spectroscopic facility for the Weizmann Astrophysical Observatory in the Negev Desert, Israel. MAST is composed of 20 60cm F/3 prime-focus PlaneWave Instruments telescopes, operating as a flexible, cost-effective alternative to a single 3 m-class aperture. Each telescope feeds science and sky fibers through a custom coupling unit into a centralized 45-fiber quasi-slit that supports independent or combined observations. Two instruments deliver complementary capabilities: DeepSpec, a low-resolution broadband spectrograph for time-domain follow-up and object classification, and HighSpec, a high-resolution narrow-band spectrograph optimized for stellar, white dwarf, and ISM studies. MAST, currently in advanced commissioning phase, is designed for full robotic operation, fast target acquisition, and flexible scheduling, enabling efficient transient classification, stellar spectroscopy, wide surveys

Items.Authors: Johan Mazoyer, Charles Goulas, Raphaël Galicher, Fabrice Vidal, Axel Potier, Florian Ferreira, Arnaud Sevin, Clémentine Béchet, Isaac Dinis, Anthony Boccaletti, Gaël Chauvin, Fausto Cortecchia, Nicolas Galland, Caroline Kulcsár, Maud Langlois, Matteo Lombini, Julien Milli, Mamadou N'Diaye, Henri-François Raynaud, Laura Schreiber, Michel Tallon, François Wildi
Items.Title: SAXO+, the second-stage adaptive optics for SPHERE: NCPA compensation and dark hole loop with a pyramid wavefront sensing
Items.Abstract: High-contrast imaging aims to detect faint exoplanets close to their host stars. Coronagraphs suppress stellar diffraction but remain limited by optical aberrations. With advanced AO systems like SPHERE/SAXO, quasi-static speckles from non-common path aberrations (NCPA) often dominate ground-based coronagraphic images, while instrument-induced aberrations similarly limit space coronagraphs. The SAXO+ upgrade adds a second fast AO loop with a near-infrared pyramid WFS, making SPHERE the first multi-stage AO facility and a key demonstrator for future systems like ELT/PCS. We study two essential techniques: static NCPA compensation using Zernike wavefront sensing, and closed-loop dark-hole control using Pair-Wise Probing and Electric Field Conjugation. COMPASS simulations show NCPA correction restores AO-limited contrast, while dark-hole control yields up to ×100 speckle suppression. These results define the SAXO+ on-sky strategy and support future ground and space coronagraphs.

Items.Authors: Ashley D. Baker, Nemanja Jovanovic, Dimitri Mawet, William Melby, Andrew Howard, Jake Zimmer, Samuel Halverson
Items.Title: System testing and characterization of HIRAX, an ultra-narrow multi-band imager for transit spectroscopy of hot Jupiters
Items.Abstract: HIRAX is a multi-band imager for the Hale telescope using ultra-narrow bandpasses centered around the sodium doublet in order to perform transit spectroscopy of hot Jupiters. It uses three 4Å wide bandpass filters each cascaded at an angle to utilize the out-of-band reflection to image a star simultaneously in the three bands, which provides a self-reference to reduce systematic effects. The goal of HIRAX is to understand the merits and limitations with this instrument architecture. To study this, HIRAX will be tested on sky in summer of 2026 with the Hale telescope by observing well-studied hot Jupiter planets with past sodium observations. Here we present commissioning activities done for HIRAX in prep for on-sky observations of HD189733b. These activities include setting up its new filter thermal control system, testing the spectral stability of the narrowband filter bandpasses, and measuring the photometric stability in lab.

Items.Authors: Shunsuke Baba, Takao Nakagawa, Yasuhiro Hirahara, Umi Enokidani, Yuan Li, Biao Zhao, Chenhao Zhao, Ryoichi Koga, Hideo Matsuhara, Takuya Hosobata, Noboru Ebizuka, Yutaka Yamagata, Toshihiro Nakaoka, Toyoaki Suzuki, Takehiko Wada, Yuji Ikeda, Hiroshi Sasago, Hidehiro Kaneda, Koji Kawabata, Hanae Inami, Shota Notsu, Hideko Nomura
Items.Title: Development and ground-based demonstration of a CdZnTe immersion grating for space-based mid-infrared high-resolution spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: To spectroscopically resolve molecular vibrational lines from space, we are proposing the High-Resolution Spectrometer (HRS; 10–18 μm, λ/Δλ ~ 30,000) for GREX-PLUS, an ISAS/JAXA mission candidate. To downsize the HRS, we adopt a CdZnTe immersion grating (CZT-IG). CZT has high transparency and refractive index, but its use for IGs remains unexplored. To develop a CZT-IG, we are measuring the cryogenic optical properties, investigating cooling-resistant anti-reflection coatings, and exploring optimal conditions for groove processing. To verify the performance of a CZT-IG, we are developing a spectrometer for ground use. This instrument aims for HRS-level resolution with a CZT-IG. It will be installed on the 1.5-m Kanata telescope in Higashi-Hiroshima, targeting the N-band (8–13 μm). Its fully reflective optics (except for the IG) allow future expansion to the Q-band (16–26 μm) at a suitable site. This design maximizes the opportunity to test a CZT-IG for the HRS.

Items.Authors: Mohammad N. Islam, Tayron Dueck, Richard Hellyer, Gordon Lacy, Elena Bergeron, Brian Hoff, Julie Levesque-Robb, Bryan Schellenberg
Items.Title: From concept to production: the making of composite reflectors for the Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio-transient Detector
Items.Abstract: This paper outlines the development and production of composite reflectors for the Canadian Hydrogen Observatory for Radio-transient Detector (CHORD) at the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory in British Columbia. DRAO developed and now fabricates 512 six‑meter composite antennas using molds, custom jigs, fixtures, and optimized workflows to ensure manufacturing repeatability. The paper details the transition from R&D to full-scale production, addressing challenges in composite fabrication and highlighting innovations that improved reflector accuracy, reduced cost, and increased production efficiency.

Items.Authors: Garima Singh, Sébastien Vievard, Julien Lozi, Vincent Deo, Kyohoon Anh, Olivier Guyon, Sandrine juillard
Items.Title: Addressing low-wind effect with the Lyot-stop low-order wavefront sensor on SCExAO
Items.Abstract: The Low-wind effect (LWE) affects coronagraphic instruments, especially those with segmented and obstructed pupils that have spider arms, causing phase discontinuities that lead to differential pistons and tip-tilt errors under low-wind conditions. Solutions to reduce the impact of LWE have been developed in both passive mode (by coating the spider arms with low-emissivity material) and active mode using wavefront sensors. We present LLOWFS's initial on-sky measurement and control of the low-order modes observed under LWE downstream of a Lyot coronagraph in SCExAO's infrared and visible arms. We also discuss the sensor fusion of LLOWFS with the high-order WFS of SCExAO and Subaru's upgraded AO3K system, as well as several control architectures that utilize the high-density actuator capabilities of SCExAO/AO3K. Preliminary LLOWFS corrections of LWE in the coronagraphic mode are promising and could improve SCExAO’s detection sensitivity of mature exoplanets at small angles.

Items.Authors: Sunil R. Golwala, Andrew D. Beyer, Peter K. Day, Fabien M. Defrance, Adriana Gavidia, Simon Hempel-Costello, Xiaolan Huang, Junhan Kim, Jean-Marc Martin, Jack Sayers, Shibo Shu, Shiling Yu
Items.Title: Status of NEW-MUSIC, the Next-generation Extended-Wavelength MUltiband Sub/millimeter Inductance Camera
Items.Abstract: The Next-generation Extended Wavelength-MUltiband Sub/millimeter Inductance Camera (NEW-MUSIC) will be a first-of-its-kind, six-band, transmillimeter-wave ("trans-mm") polarimeter for time-domain astronomy and the study of hot, diffuse gaseous haloes, and dusty sources. NEW-MUSIC, initially reported on in [doi:10.1117/12.3021175], will employ hierarchical, phased arrays of polarization-sensitive superconducting slot-dipole antennas, coupled to photolithographic bandpass filters with six spectral bands over 80-420 GHz and Al or Ti/Al microstripline-coupled, parallel-plate capacitor, lumped-element kinetic inductance detectors. Wide-bandwidth, etched silicon structures will be used to antireflection-treat the back-illuminated focal plane. NEW-MUSIC will cost-effectively reuse much of the MUSIC instrument and will deploy to both the Greenland Telescope and the Leighton Chajnantor Telescope. We report on recent progress toward a deployment-ready instrument.

Items.Authors: Ji Hoon Kim, Myungshin Im, Hyung Mok Lee, Seo-Won Chang, Donggeun Tak, Gregory Paek, Hyeonho Choi, Donghwan Hyun, Won-Hyeong Lee
Items.Title: The 7-Dimensional Telescope and the 7-Dimensional Sky Survey: status report on final commissioning and operations practice
Items.Abstract: The 7-Dimensional Telescope (7DT) is a multi-telescope array implemented for the rapid identification of electromagnetic counterparts of gravitational-wave events and the time-series, spectral mapping of the southern sky. 7DT consists of 20 (currently, 16) 50-cm units, each providing a ~1.25deg^2 FoV. It provides IFU-like data with low spectral resolution (R=30-70) using 40 (currently, 35) medium-band filters with 25nm width spanning 400–900nm. Since achieving first light in October 2023, comprehensive commissioning has been carried out to evaluate instrument functionality and verify science capabilities. 7DT carries out the 7-Dimensional Sky Survey, a three-tiered program structured to optimize scientific objectives across varying areas, depths, and cadences: the Reference Imaging Survey, the Wide-area Time-domain Survey, and the Intensive Monitoring Survey. This presentation details the commissioned instrument status, early scientific results, and the current status of operations.

Items.Authors: Parker Fagrelius, Elana Urbach, Roberto Tighe, Fritz Mueller, Douglas Neill, Brian Johnson, Antanasia Jones, Ron Harris, Anthony Tache, Anthony Borstad, Hernan Herrera, David Jiménez Mejías, Franco Colleoni, Ian Ordenes, Eric Coughlin
Items.Title: Vera C. Rubin Observatory flatfield calibration system: final design and early performance
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory Flatfield Calibration System provides the uniform, stable, and well-characterized illumination required to calibrate the LSST Camera and Simonyi Telescope. The fully installed system combines broadband “whitelight’’ LEDs, a tunable-laser subsystem for monochromatic flats, and an f/4 projector with an aspheric reflector that illuminates a 10-m Lambertian screen. A comprehensive monitoring suite, including a NIST-calibrated photodiode with electrometer readout and fiber-fed spectrographs, tracks illumination stability and spectral content. Key thermal and electrical considerations, such as laser temperature control and power distribution for the distributed system, are incorporated into the final design. Early commissioning results indicate that the flatfield calibration system performance meets the requirements for LSST Camera characterization and early Rubin Observatory operations.

Items.Authors: Evan P. Bray
Items.Title: Characterization of a first-generation parabolic deformable mirror
Items.Abstract: Existing state-of-the-art wavefront sensing and control setups for the imaging of exoplanets utilize two high-actuator count flat deformable mirrors (DMs) to control both phase and amplitude aberrations. One of the objectives of the Exoplanet Spectroscopy (ExoSpec) project at Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) is to improve upon this regime through the development of parabolic deformable mirrors (PDMs), which can address several of the key limitations in existing setups. Specifically, the need for flat DMs to be located in conjugate pupil planes drives unique packaging challenges that can be overcome by allowing the off-axis imaging elements to be controllable as well. In addition, simulations show that the use of deformable powered elements will increase the overall controllable bandwidth, up to 35% over 5-12 Lambda/D. To pursue this effort, the ExoSpec group has worked with Bertin Alpao to produce a first-generation parabolic DM.

Items.Authors: Sophia Da Costa, Albert Lau, Keith Vanderlinde
Items.Title: Low-cost, ultra-wideband, differential low-noise amplifier for interferometric radio telescopes
Items.Abstract: Many feeds used in radio astronomy are inherently differential and are typically interfaced with conventional single-ended receiver systems. Given the rising cost of 50-ohm coaxial cable coupled with the growing interest in differential signal transmission techniques, the development of low-loss, low-cost differential amplifiers is well-motivated for up-and-coming interferometric arrays. We present a low-cost, ultra-wideband differential low-noise amplifier (LNA) that eliminates the need for a pre-amplification balun. Built entirely from commercial surface-mount components, the LNA costs ~$20 USD per unit with a noise figure less than 0.3 dB across a 10:1 bandwidth. On-sky results of a single-polarized version demonstrate noise temperatures as low as 25 K when matched to a ~110-ohm Vivalid feed across its operational band of 300-1500 MHz. This talk details the design, modifications, and testing of the updated dual-polarized model.

Items.Authors: Jay K. Kueny, Jared R. Males, Alycia J. Weinberger, Maggie Y. Kautz, Joseph D. Long, Laird M. Close, Sebastiaan Haffert, Alexander Hedglen, Parker T. Johnson, Katie Twitchell, Eden McEwen, Jialin Li, Joshua Liberman, Miles Lucas, Tiffany Nguyen, Avalon Gower, Lauren Schatz, Elena Tonucci, Matthijs Mars, Olivier Guyon
Items.Title: WindsoCC: reconstructing the wind-driven halo in MagAO-X images using wavefront sensor telemetry
Items.Abstract: The wind-driven halo (WDH) is a persistant noise artifact that arises due to the servo-lag inherent to all adaptive optics (AO) instruments and especially plagues images of extended objects. However, since wavefront sensors (WFSs) continuously track the closed-loop residual wavefront error, WFS telemetry presents as the ideal resource for removing this type of noise artifact. Using WFS telemetry from MagAO-X, which is the extreme AO imager for the 6.5-meter Magellan Clay telescope, we present a new software tool for WDH reconstruction and removal. Since MagAO-X's WFS images are saved during data acquisition, we detail how our new tool, windsoCC, cross-correlates the recorded closed-loop wavefront to characterize several individual layers of the atmosphere above Las Campanas Observatory. We then make use of the wind parameters learned through windsoCC to reconstruct and remove the WDH in individual MagAO-X science images using a parametric model.

Items.Authors: Costanza Bellucci, Paolo de Bernardis, Luca Lamagna, Vipul Prasad Maranchery, Silvia Masi, Alessandro Paiella, Giorgio Pettinari
Items.Title: Design of a KID-based on-chip FTS spectrometer for astrophysical applications
Items.Abstract: We present the design of a W-band (75-110 GHz) on-chip Fourier Transform Spectrometer integrated with a titanium-aluminum Kinetic Inductance Detector (KID) on a silicon substrate, aimed at compact, cryogenically compatible imaging spectroscopy for millimeter-wave astronomy. The device combines a planar antenna, an on-chip FTS, and the KID. Simulations indicate low reflection, stable isolation across the band, and tunable spectral resolution. Superconducting thin films of niobium and niobium nitride were characterized to optimize design of the antenna and the integrated FTS. A first antenna-coupled KID prototype consisting of 37 pixels was tested at 150 mK, validating the antenna and KID subsystem performance and demonstrating the feasibility of scalable, space-ready spectrometers for astrophysical and cosmological observations.

Items.Authors: Pedro J. Amado González, Jesús Aceituno Castro, the Photonic EMARCOT collaboration, Miguel Andrés Sánchez-Carrasdo, Stefan Cikota, Marina Centenera Merino, Javier Flores, David Pérez Medialdea, María Isabel Ruiz-López, Kalaga Madhav, Julius Göhring, Abani Shankar Nayak, Francisco José Pozuelos-Romero, Sergio León-Saval, José Luis Ortiz Moreno, Martin Roth
Items.Title: Photonic EMARCOT at Calar Alto: a modular and photonically-connected telescope architecture for the post-ELT era
Items.Abstract: Photonic EMARCOT is a new modular telescope initiative led by IAA-CSIC and the Calar Alto Observatory (CAHA, ICTS). The project aims to replace traditional monolithic telescope with scalable architectures composed of multiple telescope units linked through photonic technologies. This approach enables increased collecting area, improved sensitivity, and the ability to route starlight to several instruments simultaneously. The strategic roadmap includes a first 5-metre-equivalent module by 2030 and a 15-metre-class configuration by combining several modules by 2035. Positioned within CAHA’s long-term plan and aligned with European research-infrastructure priorities, Photonic EMARCOT invites new partners to contribute to the development of this modular and photonically connected telescope system and its instrumentation. This contribution outlines the project’s scientific motivations, system architecture, and collaborative framework.

Items.Authors: Steven Li, Pablo Trujillo, Jason VazBrown, Javier Romualdez, John Hartley
Items.Title: Generative-design-driven gondola for the POEMM balloon telescope: adapting topology optimization for truss fabrication
Items.Abstract: StarSpec developed the Gondola Element (GE) for POEMM’s 1.8-m Nasmyth balloon telescope. To achieve this, we implemented a Fusion 360 generative-design pipeline that optimizes component placement to minimize the structural envelope and balance about the azimuth pivot. The pipeline incorporates OTE-driven keep-outs,remote-mass attachment sites, enumerates certification and flight load cases, and performs multi-case gradient-based optimization on the worst-case load. To ensure the resulting organic topology is manufacturable at 20-ft scale, we introduce a homogenized material model representing beam-and-sheet assemblies. We utilized a rule-based skeletonization / memberization workflow to convert organic topology outputs into standard beam/panel architectures, supported by a parameterized, scripted design loop to minimize redesign effort. The final memberized GE meets POEMM’s structural, modal, and opto-mechanical targets.

Items.Authors: Wesley Newton
Items.Title: Phase change over ambient temperature evaluation of various coaxial cables at 15.4 GHz for use on the MeerKAT radio telescope array
Items.Abstract: This paper presents a comparative evaluation of phase change versus ambient temperature for multiple high performance coaxial cables at 15.4 GHz. This evaluation was carried out to select the optimum cable for the new Band 5b capability to be added to the MeerKAT radio telescope array. A test method was proposed, carried out and further refined. Findings inform optimal cable selection for high-precision radio astronomy, where phase stability is critical for array calibration and imaging performance. The result is a tabled comparison of a range of high performance coaxial cables characterised over temperature from -5C to +40C.

Items.Authors: Lee R. Spitler, Zhemin Cai, Mark Casali, Timothy Chin, Chris Coote, Peter Dekker, Tobias Feger, Anthony Horton, Yevgen Kripak, Jon Lawrence, Helen McGregor, Scott Smedley, Sana Syed, Lew Waller, Yizheng Wang, Jessica Zheng
Items.Title: Space-ready optics from AAO: thermal imaging, navigation, and agile pointing
Items.Abstract: Australian Astronomical Optics (AAO) at Macquarie University is leveraging its heritage in astronomical instrumentation to develop space-ready optical systems for navigation and imaging. We review three recent milestones: Malya, a space-qualified thermal imaging payload delivered to Gilmour Space for Earth observation; ALOHA, a precision optical head enabling LiDAR-like navigation for lunar landings; and OWL, a linkage-driven fast steering mirror system for agile pointing of large-aperture imaging payloads. These projects demonstrate AAO’s ability to adapt telescope technologies for space missions through innovative design and qualification. We conclude with future directions, including scalable pointing systems and advanced optical payloads with potential flow-back benefits for next-generation astronomical instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Jared R. Males, Laird M. Close, Olivier Guyon, Olivier Durney, Maggie Kautz, Louis Desdoigts, Matthijs Mars, Elena Tonucci, Adam K. Taras, Yinzi Xin, Rico Landman
Items.Title: The final design of GMagAO-X: the wavefront sensing and control (WFS&C) architecture of GMagAO-X
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Adaptive Optics eXtreme (GMagAO-X) instrument has now been selected as an official part of the Giant Magellan Telescope’s (GMT) instrument suite. The instrument will be ready at first-light of the GMT in the mid 2030s. The instrument is now progressing towards its final design with a final design review planned for March, 2027. The high-density actuator deformable mirror with 21.000 actuators will allow GMagAO-X to create diffraction-limited images from visible to near-infrared. GMagAO-X will be coupled with high-performance coronagraphs to search for exoplanets at the diffraction-limit. The coronagraphs require wavefront control at sub-nm precision. We will provide an update on the wavefront sensing and control architecture and how the loops interact with each other through end-to-end simulations.

Items.Authors: Wojciech Golebiowski, Przemysław Bartczak, Krzysztof Kaminski, Monika Kaminska, Tomasz Kwiatkowski, Michal Witkowski, Adam Popowicz, Peter Dobusch, Luca Conversi, Jose Villavilla, Ernesto Dölling
Items.Title: A modular wide-field observatory node for distributed NEO survey networks
Items.Abstract: We present a modular, autonomous observatory node designed as the core element of a scalable telescope array for NEO and space-debris monitoring. Each node incorporates two independent 0.6 m f/1.7 telescopes equipped with large-format IMX411 sCMOS cameras and motorized Sloan filter sliders, enabling simultaneous survey and follow-up, multi-band imaging, and high-SNR stacking. The goal is to achieve unfiltered 21 mag detection within 60 s exposure. The system integrates weather-aware safety logic, redundant monitoring, industrial-grade control architecture, and sub-millisecond time synchronization. The prototype will be validated at a Southern European site. The design provides a deployable, COTS-based foundation for future geographically distributed survey network and observations and processing service built on it.

Items.Authors: Stefanie Brackenhoff, Akira Endo, Shinji Fujita, Shiro Ikeda, Kenichi Karatsu, Kotaro Kohno, Arend Moerman, Yuri Nishimura, Matus Rybak, Tatsuya Takekoshi, Yoichi Tamura, Akio Taniguchi, Javier Aguilera, Hiroki Akamatsu, Tom Bakx, Bruno Buijtendorp, Scott Cray, Shahab Dabironezare, Yasunori Fujii, Sho Fujisawa, Kazuyuki Fujita, Masato Hagimoto, Shaul Hanany, Shunsuke Honda, Shuji Hotta, Robert Huiting, Takahiro Iino, Chihiro Imamura, Shuhei Inoue, Akira Inoue, Shutaro Inui, Shun Ishii, Yuji Ishizaki, Kotaro Iwakami, Masato Kato, Ryohei Kawabe, Nick de Keijzer, Tetsu Kitayama, Micah Klettke, Toshihiko Kobiki, Ryoya Kojima, Kuniaki Konishi, Ryusuke Koriyama, Hosun Lee, Fumiya Maeda, Louis Marting, Tomotake Matsumura, Ren Matsusaka, Tetsuhiro Minamidani, Kana Morokuma, Vignesh Murugesan, Maki Nagata, Shunichi Nakatsubo, Kanako Narita, Rallou Nikolopoulou, Kazushige Ohtawara, Norika Okauchi, Leon Olde Scholtenhuis, Tai Oshima, Alejandro Pascual Laguna, Madelief Peters, Lucie Rowland, Masaki Sakakibara, Seiichi Sakamoto, Haruyuki Sakurai, Yuma Sato, Mizuki Sato, Mahoshi Sawamura, Fenno Steenvoorde, Ryota Takaku, David Thoen, Huckleberry Thums, Akiyoshi Tsujita, Hideki Umehata, Shinsuke Uno, Sten Vollebregt, Kazuki Watanabe, Paul van der Werf, Doreen Wernicke, Beth Westoby, Juri Yamanaka, Stephen Yates, Jochem Baselmans
Items.Title: Galaxy observations with DESHIMA 2.0
Items.Abstract: DESHIMA 2.0 is an integrated superconducting spectrometer operating between 200 and 400 GHz with 339 spectral channels. Its deployment on the ASTE 10-m telescope marks a step forward for wide-band (sub)millimeter instruments that use MKID filterbanks with compact optics.    To fully exploit DESHIMA 2.0's capabilities, we are developing a dedicated position-switching analysis pipeline, tailored to the stability requirements of on-chip spectrometers. Position switching offers an alternative to scanning-based observing modes, with increased sensitivity for unresolved targets such as high-redshift dusty star-forming galaxies. These are a key science driver for DESHIMA 2.0, because its octave-bandwidth offers a unique window into the bright [C II] line at 3≲z≲7.    We present the calibration and analysis pipeline, highlight lessons learned, and outline strategies relevant to upcoming systems using similar observing modes. We show performance metrics and early astronomical results.

Items.Authors: Ian Hendricksen, Jean-François Cliche, Matt Dobbs
Items.Title: Commissioning of the CHORD F‑engine and system validation with a fully FPGA-based F‑X correlator
Items.Abstract: The Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio-transient Detector (CHORD) is achieving rapid progress in the construction of its first 64 dishes at the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory (DRAO) in British Columbia, Canada. We present an overview of an RFSoC-based F-Engine implemented on the t0.CRS platform for CHORD and detail current commissioning efforts for the first CHORD dishes. We describe the installation of a single F-Engine crate connected to the first fully-instrumented CHORD dishes, enabling the collection of preliminary datasets for system-level performance testing. To validate the CHORD F-Engine, we have developed a complementary version of its firmware which implements a complete X-engine onboard the FPGA alongside the F-engine for a subset of the feeds. We demonstrate the initial success of the CHORD F-Engine by conducting an observation of a bright radio calibrator source using our fully FPGA-based single-board F-X correlator.

Items.Authors: Picha Ruenarrom, Carolyn Atkins, Krittapas Chanchaiworawit, Tarathon Intaros, Younes Chahid, Valentina Oyarzun, Scott McPhee, Luca Millan, Samattachai Tanun, Teerawat Kuha, Auychai Laoyang, Manlika Pinkaew, Apichat Leckngam
Items.Title: Comparative SPDT machinability and surface quality of cast aluminum and additively manufactured aluminum for lightweight components in space missions
Items.Abstract: We present a preliminary comparison of the SPDT machinability of five aluminum substrates: RSA aluminum, cast Al 6061, 3D-printed Scalmalloy, HIP-treated Scalmalloy, and 3D-printed AlSi10Mg. All samples were machined under identical ultra-precision conditions, followed by form-error measurement, nanometer-scale roughness evaluation, and microstructural inspection. The study compares porosity, print defects, scratches, and surface roughness among the additively manufactured variants against RSA and cast Al 6061, highlighting the improved homogeneity and reduced porosity from HIP treatment. These results support the use of high-strength additively manufactured aluminum for lightweight monolithic optical structures in space applications, reducing reliance on bimetallic thermal-compensation designs and improving thermoelastic stability and system simplicity.

Items.Authors: Rico Landman, Sebastiaan Haffert, Joseph Long, Jared Males, Matthijs Mars, Liam Koning, Laird Close, Warren Foster, Kyle Van Gorkom, Olivier Guyon, Alexander Hedglen, Parker Johnson, Maggie Kautz, Jay Kueny, Jialin Li, Joshua Liberman, Miles Lucas, Jennifer Lumbres, Eden McEwen, Avalon McLeod, Lauren Schatz, Elena Tonucci, Katie Twitchell
Items.Title: No need to modulate: on-sky results of a neural network enhanced pyramid wavefront sensor and prospects for the ELT’s
Items.Abstract: One of the main limitations of ground-based extreme adaptive optics systems (XAO) is the balance between the temporal and photon noise error. The unmodulated Pyramid Wavefront Sensor (uPWFS) promises significant gains in sensitivity over its modulated counterpart, but its practical use is limited by its linearity range. Nonlinear reconstructors provide a pathway to recover this dynamic range while preserving the sensitivity of the uPWFS, thereby reducing photon noise and improving contrast. We present the real-time implementation of a Neural Network (NN) reconstructor and show on-sky results with MagAO-X, demonstrating robust and stable correction across diverse atmospheric conditions. Furthermore, simulations of NN-enhanced uPWFS operation on future Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs) predict substantial gains for high-contrast imaging. These results validate NN-enhanced wavefront sensing as a promising, ready-to-deploy technology for next-generation high-contrast instruments.

Items.Authors: Oliver Jeong, Michel Piat, Aritoki Suzuki
Items.Title: High efficiency millimeter-wave on-chip spectrometer
Items.Abstract: We have developed a novel on-chip filterbank spectrometer for millimeter-wave astrophysics and dark matter searches. The filterbank utilizes superconducting resonators built on a low loss dielectric to achieve a high spectral resolution spectrometer across a millimeter wave frequency range. This filterbank architecture overcomes the 50% channel efficiency limit imposed by conventional filterbank designs used by multiple groups working on on-chip spectrometers.  This spectrometer serves as the key technology for detection of emission lines from large scale structure of the universe, mass discrimination for broadband axion search instruments, and background characterization of low-threshold dark matter experiments. We present on the design, performance, and applications of this novel technology.

Items.Authors: Victoria Laidlaw, Felipe Guzmán, Nicolás Hernández, Esteban Vera Rojas
Items.Title: Neural NOPE: A physics-informed neural network approach to mitigate nonlinearity in pyramid wavefront sensing for adaptive optics
Items.Abstract: Pyramid wavefront sensors (PWFSs) are key components of adaptive optics (AO) systems for next-generation extremely large telescopes (ELTs). However, their nonlinear behavior can degrade image quality under strong atmospheric turbulence, especially when conventional matrix vector multiplication (MVM) methods are used.  To address this, we introduce a hybrid approach that combines a model-based reconstructor, called nonlinear pyramid extension (NOPE), with a physics-informed unrolling architecture. Compared to the standard NOPE, the new neural NOPE accelerates convergence, enhances reconstruction fidelity and improves robustness while preserving physical interpretability.  Comparisons show that neural NOPE effectively mitigates PWFS nonlinearity under severe turbulence, outperforming standard MVM approaches in such conditions.

Items.Authors: Yuan Ren
Items.Title: Terahertz spectroscopy with compact metasurface spectrometer
Items.Abstract: Terahertz (THz) spectroscopy is of great significance due to the rich molecular and atomic fingerprint lines in this frequency regime, supporting impactful applications in materials science, biology, and astronomy. Leveraging advances in metasurface engineering, we have developed a compact THz spectrometer that integrates a phase grating and two transmissive metasurfaces on a single platform. By suppressing chromatic dispersion and angular aberrations, the device forms a parallel focal plane, enabling straightforward coupling to detector arrays. Operating from 1.23 THz to 1.43 THz, the spectrometer achieves a spectral resolution of 21 GHz, corresponding to a resolution factor of 63 (f/Δf).

Items.Authors: Barnaby R. M. Norris, Sergio G. Leon-Saval, Christopher H. Betters, Adam Taras, Yoo Jung Kim, Jonathan Lin, Justin Vella, Jin Wei, Yinzi Xin, Sébastien Vievard, Daniel S. Dahl, Akira Rodziewicz-Ryan, Nathan K. Long, Andrew Ross-Adams, Michael P. Fitzgerald, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Jared Males, Laird M. Close, Nemanja Jovanovic, Vincent Déo, Julien Lozi, Olivier Guyon
Items.Title: The photonic-lantern wavefront sensor and coherent-differential-imager: the next step in full-wave photonic-lantern sensing
Items.Abstract: In recent years the use of the photonic lantern (PL) as a wavefront sensor has seen an explosion of interest, due to its sensitivity to petal and low-wind-effect modes, NCPA resilience, detector efficiency, and spectral resolution. Now, new advances allow the PL to sense far more than just the wavefront: by using an ‘oversampled’ PL (where the number of output fibres exceeds the number of input modes) the complete focal-plane electric field can be measured, including coherence. This enables wavelength-resolved, super-diffraction-limited imaging with speckles removed, essentially ‘undoing’ the seeing. We present the latest on-sky results from the PL wavefront sensor and laboratory results demonstrating the oversampled PL’s coherent-differential-imaging capabilities. We also present details of the multi-headed neural network that enables this, and the development of on-sky instruments designed to exploit this mode including for SCExAO and the Photonic Wavefront Imager (PWI) for MagAO-X.
